questions.prompt: With the coin that lands heads 60% of the time, you stake 40% of your money each round. What happens over 100 rounds?
options: You end with 0.78 of your money, because each loss at 0.6 hurts more than each win at 1.4 helps
You grow fastest, because 40% has the largest expected value per round
You end with exactly what you started with, because the wins and losses cancel
You lose everything on the first tail
questions.explanation: The average log growth at 40% is −0.00245 per round, so 100 rounds give a growth factor of 0.78, a loss of 22%. The expected value is positive, but compounding punishes the large losses.

questions.prompt: A bet wins 50% of the time and pays 3 for each 1 staked. What fraction does the Kelly criterion stake?
questions.explanation: f = p − q / b = 0.5 − 0.5 / 3 = 0.33. The value 0.17 is only q / b, the part you subtract from p.

questions.prompt: Why does the Kelly criterion maximise the average log growth instead of the average gain per bet?
options: Because logarithms make the numbers smaller and easier to print
Because your money compounds, so what you end with is the product of growth factors, and logs turn that product into a sum
Because the average gain per bet is always negative
Because the average gain ignores the chance of winning
questions.explanation: Each round multiplies your money by 1 + f or 1 − f. Adding the logs of those growth factors is the same as multiplying them, so the stake with the highest average log growth ends with the most money.
